title: Circuit Calculations & Behaviour
description: Series and parallel circuits, Ohm's law (V = IR), Watt's law (P = IV), AC vs DC, and signal waveforms.
content_html:
Electron Flow in Circuits

Electric current in a conductor is caused by the movement of electrons. In a metal wire, free electrons drift from the negative terminal of the supply towards the positive terminal — this is called electron flow. Conventional current, used in circuit diagrams and calculations, is defined as flowing from positive to negative, which is the opposite direction. For all OCR calculations you use conventional current direction, but you should be aware that actual electron flow goes the other way.

Series and Parallel Circuits

In a series circuit, components are connected in a single loop. The same current flows through every component, but the supply voltage is shared between them. The total resistance of a series circuit is simply the sum of all individual resistances: R_total = R1 + R2 + R3. If three resistors of 10 Ω, 20 Ω, and 30 Ω are connected in series, the total resistance is 60 Ω.

In a parallel circuit, components are connected across the same two nodes. Every component receives the full supply voltage, and the total current is the sum of the currents through each branch. The total resistance of a parallel circuit is lower than any individual resistor. For two resistors: 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2. For three resistors: 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. Always find 1/R_total first, then take the reciprocal to get R_total.

Key Fact

Series: R_total = R1 + R2 + R3 (resistances add directly). Parallel (up to three resistors): 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 — always take the reciprocal of your final sum to get R_total. The OCR specification covers a maximum of three resistors in either configuration.

Ohm's Law: V = I × R

Ohm's law states that the potential difference across a component is directly proportional to the current through it, provided temperature is constant. The formula is V = I × R, where V is voltage in volts (V), I is current in amps (A), and R is resistance in ohms (Ω). You must be able to rearrange this formula: I = V ÷ R to find current; R = V ÷ I to find resistance. For example, if a resistor has 12 V across it and a current of 0.5 A flows through it, its resistance is R = 12 ÷ 0.5 = 24 Ω.

Watt's Law: P = I × V

The power dissipated by a component equals the current through it multiplied by the voltage across it: P = I × V, where P is power in watts (W). This formula can be rearranged: I = P ÷ V; V = P ÷ I. For example, a motor operating at 6 V and drawing a current of 2 A has a power consumption of P = 2 × 6 = 12 W. Remove the sentence 'Note that OCR explicitly excludes P = I² × R from the specification — you only need P = I × V.' Replace with: 'P = I × V is the formula most directly tested; the derived forms P = I²R and P = V²/R can be used when voltage is not directly given — check your specification formula sheet to confirm which forms are supplied in the exam.'

Key Fact

Ohm's law: V = I × R (V in volts, I in amps, R in ohms). Watt's law: P = I × V (P in watts). Both formulas must be used with base units — convert any kΩ or mA to Ω or A before substituting. Remove 'OCR does not require P = I² × R.' Teach P = IV as primary; note that derived forms are also standard.

AC and DC: Types of Current

Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only; its voltage remains constant over time. Batteries supply DC. Alternating current (AC) repeatedly reverses direction; the voltage rises and falls in a regular cycle. The UK mains supply is AC at 230 V, 50 Hz. Most electronic circuits use DC internally, but mains power is AC — a transformer and rectifier convert AC to DC in a mains adaptor.

Analogue and Digital Signals

An analogue signal varies continuously and can take any value within a range — like the output of a microphone or a temperature sensor. A digital signal takes only two discrete states: high (1) or low (0). The waveforms for these signals look very different: an analogue signal produces a smooth sine wave with a continuous range of amplitudes, while a digital signal produces a square wave that switches sharply between two voltage levels. Key waveform properties include: amplitude (the peak height of the wave), frequency (the number of complete cycles per second in Hz), and periodic time (the duration of one complete cycle, T = 1 ÷ f).

Three resistors — 10 Ω, 20 Ω, and 40 Ω — are connected in parallel. Find the total resistance. Step 1: 1/R_total = 1/10 + 1/20 + 1/40 Step 2: Convert to a common denominator of 40: 4/40 + 2/40 + 1/40 = 7/40 Step 3: R_total = 40 ÷ 7 ≈ 5.71 Ω Notice that the total resistance (5.71 Ω) is less than the smallest individual resistor (10 Ω) — this is always true in a parallel circuit. Show all three steps in exam working to maximise method marks.

Analogue signals capture the full continuous range of a measurement, which can mean higher fidelity — a microphone output faithfully follows every nuance of sound. However, analogue signals are susceptible to noise: any interference adds to the signal and cannot easily be removed. Digital signals can be regenerated perfectly from their two-state nature — if a signal is noisy but clearly above the threshold, a circuit can restore it to a clean 1. Digital signals are also easier to process, store, and transmit reliably, which is why almost all modern communication and computing systems use digital formats. The trade-off is that converting from analogue to digital (via an ADC) introduces a small quantisation error — the continuous signal is approximated in discrete steps.
exam_tip_html: For Ohm's law and power calculations, always convert units to base units before substituting: mA to A (÷1000), kΩ to Ω (×1000). Show your working in three clear steps — formula, substitution, answer with unit — because OCR awards method marks even if the final value is wrong. For parallel resistance, a very common error is forgetting to take the reciprocal at the end: after finding 1/R_total, divide 1 by that value to get R_total in Ω.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • In a series circuit R_total = R1 + R2 + R3; in a parallel circuit 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 — always take the reciprocal to get R_total, and always check it is less than the smallest individual resistor.
  • Ohm's law (V = I × R) and Watt's law (P = I × V) must be rearranged to find any variable — convert all values to base units first and show formula, substitution, and answer with unit in exam working.
  • AC reverses direction cyclically (mains = 230 V, 50 Hz); DC flows in one direction (batteries). Digital signals are two-state and noise-resistant; analogue signals are continuous but susceptible to interference.

glossary_terms.definition: Negatively charged subatomic particles that carry electric current by drifting through a conductor from the negative terminal to the positive terminal.
A circuit in which all components are connected end-to-end in a single loop, so the same current flows through every component.
A circuit in which components are connected across the same two nodes, so each component has the same voltage across it but draws its own current.
The time taken for one complete cycle of a waveform, calculated as T = 1 ÷ f, where f is frequency in hertz.

practice_questions.text:
Which formula correctly states Ohm's law?
A) V = I + R
B) V = I × R
C) V = I ÷ R
D) V = R ÷ I
State two differences between alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC).
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: AC reverses direction periodically / DC flows in one direction only; AC voltage varies (rises and falls in a cycle) / DC voltage is constant; mains supply is AC / batteries supply DC. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A resistor has a potential difference of 9 V across it and a current of 30 mA flowing through it. Calculate the resistance of the resistor. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: converts 30 mA to 0.030 A (or equivalent correct method). 1 mark: substitutes correctly into R = V ÷ I: R = 9 ÷ 0.030. 1 mark: correct answer = 300 Ω (unit required). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A circuit contains two resistors connected in parallel: R1 = 12 Ω and R2 = 6 Ω. The supply voltage is 12 V.

Describe how to calculate the total resistance and use it to calculate the total current drawn from the supply.
practice_questions.marks:
Parallel resistance (2 marks): 1/R_total = 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/12 + 2/12 = 3/12; R_total = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 Ω (1 mark for correct formula application; 1 mark for correct R_total = 4 Ω with unit).
Current calculation (2 marks): I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 4; I = 3 A (1 mark for correct substitution; 1 mark for correct answer 3 A with unit). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student is designing a portable LED torch. The torch uses two AA batteries (each 1.5 V) in series and the LED circuit draws a current of 20 mA.

Discuss the key circuit considerations the student should take into account when designing the torch.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): balanced discussion with at least two developed factors. For example: total supply voltage = 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 V; the student must calculate the series resistor needed to limit current to 20 mA — using V = I × R (with the voltage dropped across the resistor = supply voltage minus Change 'LED forward voltage ≈ 2 V if LED Vf ≈ 1 V, R = 2 ÷ 0.020 = 100 Ω' to 'LED forward voltage (Vf) for a typical red LED ≈ 2 V; voltage across resistor = 3 − 2 = 1 V; R = 1 ÷ 0.020 = 50 Ω (accept any value using a realistic Vf of 1.8–2.2 V with correct arithmetic)') — this prevents the LED from burning out (first factor, developed with calculation). Contrasted with: power consumption affects battery life — P = I × V = 0.020 × 3 = 0.06 W means the batteries will drain over time, so the student must consider capacity and efficiency in the design (second factor, developed with calculation and application to the scenario).
Secure (3–4 marks): two factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): one factor identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): a single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A factory uses a 24 V DC motor to drive a conveyor belt. The motor has a resistance of 8 Ω and draws a current of 3 A at full load.

Evaluate the suitability of using direct current (DC) for this application compared to alternating current (AC), using your knowledge of circuit behaviour and calculations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): a balanced evaluation supported by calculations and application to the factory scenario. Arguments for DC: motors in control systems require a constant, predictable current direction — a DC motor's speed and torque are directly controllable via voltage (V = I × R gives 24 = 3 × 8 Ω, consistent with spec), and DC power P = I × V = 3 × 24 = 72 W is constant and predictable. DC from a battery/PSU also means the motor is independent of mains supply fluctuations. Arguments for AC consideration: mains supply is AC (230 V, 50 Hz) so the factory's power infrastructure is AC — powering a DC motor from AC requires a rectifier and voltage regulation circuit, adding complexity and cost. In high-power industrial applications, AC motors can be more robust and cheaper to maintain. Counter: for precision conveyor control, DC is widely preferred because speed can be varied by simply varying voltage; AC motor speed is fundamentally tied to mains frequency, requiring a frequency inverter to vary speed. A clear, substantiated judgement: DC is the more suitable choice for this precision, controlled-speed conveyor application, though it requires appropriate power conversion from the mains AC supply.
Secure (5–6 marks): arguments on both sides with calculations and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): relevant points with limited calculations, largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): basic points, no evaluation or judgement. [8 marks]

left: Total resistance lower than any branch

flashcard_questions.q: State Ohm's law as a formula, including the units of each symbol.
flashcard_questions.a: Ohm's law is V = I × R: V in volts, I in amps, R in ohms.

flashcard_questions.q: State Watt's law as a formula, including the units of each symbol.
flashcard_questions.a: Watt's law is P = I × V: P in watts, I in amps, V in volts.

flashcard_questions.q: How is total resistance calculated in a series circuit with three resistors?
flashcard_questions.a: In a series circuit, total resistance equals R1 + R2 + R3, adding all values directly.

flashcard_questions.q: How is total resistance calculated in a parallel circuit with two resistors?
flashcard_questions.a: Use 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2, then take the reciprocal to find R_total.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the direction of conventional current compared to electron flow?
flashcard_questions.a: Conventional current flows from positive to negative, which is opposite to actual electron flow direction.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between AC and DC current?
flashcard_questions.a: DC flows in one direction only; AC periodically reverses direction in a repeating cycle.

flashcard_questions.q: A resistor has 12 V across it and 0.4 A through it. What is its resistance?
flashcard_questions.a: Using R = V ÷ I: R = 12 ÷ 0.4 = 30 Ω.

flashcard_questions.q: A 5 Ω component carries 2 A. What is the power it dissipates?
flashcard_questions.a: No arithmetic correction needed. Flagged for consistency only — this should be resolved by correcting the P=I²R exclusion claim in the main text (see HIGH findings above).

flashcard_questions.q: What waveform shape does an analogue signal produce?
flashcard_questions.a: An analogue signal produces a smooth, continuously varying sine wave shape.

flashcard_questions.q: What waveform shape does a digital signal produce?
flashcard_questions.a: A digital signal produces a square wave that switches sharply between two voltage levels.

flashcard_questions.q: What is periodic time and how is it calculated?
flashcard_questions.a: Periodic time (T) is the duration of one complete wave cycle, calculated as T = 1 ÷ f.

flashcard_questions.q: In a parallel circuit, what happens to the total resistance compared to individual resistors?
flashcard_questions.a: Total resistance in a parallel circuit is always less than the smallest individual resistor value.
